mainTopic: How an idol's forbidden status is cancelled (ביטול עבודה זרה): shared idols, damage versus insults, and selling the idol to a Jewish or gentile smith.
overview: The amud finishes רבי הלל בריה דרבי וולס's teaching about an idol shared by a Jew and a gentile. Only the gentile can nullify his own share, and the Jew's share stays forbidden forever. A new משנה teaches that damaging an idol nullifies it, even just crushing its face. Insults like spitting or throwing dung do not nullify it. רבי and חכמים argue about whether selling or mortgaging the idol nullifies it. חזקיה uses פסוקים from ישעיהו to show that a worshipper who curses his idol in anger goes back to it. Two אמוראים disagree about whether the selling dispute concerns a gentile smith or a Jewish smith. A ברייתא of רבי is brought as a proof, but the proof is pushed off. A challenge from a ברייתא about scrap metal is answered: that seller never knowingly sold an idol. A new ברייתא about idols that were pawned, buried, stolen or abandoned begins, and its ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The case is a shared idol
steps.stepSummary: רבי הלל בריה דרבי וולס explains that the משנה's rule is needed for an idol that a gentile and a Jew own together. Only the gentile can nullify his own share.
steps.simpleTranslation: [רבי הלל son] of רבי וולס said: It is needed only where he has a partnership in it. It teaches us that a Jew cannot nullify a gentile's idol, but a gentile can nullify his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering why the משנה needed to say something that seemed obvious, that a Jew cannot nullify a gentile's idol. The answer is that the משנה is talking about an idol shared by a Jew and a gentile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By itself, the rule that a Jew cannot nullify a gentile's idol sounds too obvious to need saying. The new point concerns partnership: even when the Jew owns part of the idol, he still cannot nullify it. The gentile partner, though, can nullify his own share.

keyTerms.meaning: 'it was needed only for...'; tells us which special case a rule is about
'it teaches us'; introduces the new point
nullifies; removes the idol's forbidden status

phrases.english: of Rabbi Volas:
phrases.notes: This is the end of a line that started on the previous daf: 'Rabbi Hillel, son of Rabbi Volas, said.'

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נִצְרְכָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בָּהּ שׁוּתָּפוּת,
phrases.english: It is needed only where he has a partnership in it,
phrases.notes: The idol belongs partly to a Jew and partly to a gentile.

phrases.english: and it teaches us
that it is a Jew who cannot nullify a gentile's [idol],
but a gentile can nullify his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא נִצְרְכָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בָּהּ שׁוּתָּפוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'isn't this obvious?' question from the previous daf about the משנה's rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the rule in a specific case (a shared idol).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule seemed too obvious to need saying.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that in a shared idol, only the gentile can nullify his own share; the Jew cannot nullify the gentile's share.

steps.title: Another version: the ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן מנסיא
steps.stepSummary: Some attach רבי הלל's explanation to a ברייתא instead. In that ברייתא, רבי שמעון בן מנסיא says a Jew's idol can never be nullified.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are those who teach it on a ברייתא. רבי שמעון בן מנסיא says: An idol of a Jew can never be nullified.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a second version of where רבי הלל's explanation belongs. It sets up the ברייתא that his explanation will be attached to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, רבי הלל's words explain a ברייתא, not the משנה. The ברייתא says a Jew's idol has no ביטול 'ever', and that word 'ever' will be questioned next.

keyTerms.meaning: 'some teach it'; introduces a second version of where a statement belongs
a teaching from the time of the משנה that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: There are those who teach it on a ברייתא,
phrases.notes: 'It' means רבי הלל's explanation from the previous step.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says:
An idol of a Jew
can never be nullified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different version of where רבי הלל's explanation applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew's idol can never be nullified.

steps.title: Why the word 'never'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the extra word עולמית ('never') adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'never' come to add?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא added the strong word 'never'. This question sets up רבי הלל's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is already known that a Jew cannot nullify his own idol. So the word 'never' must be adding a special case.

phrases.english: What does 'never' mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions one word in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case does the extra word 'never' include?

steps.title: Even with a gentile partner, the Jew's share stays forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבי הלל says 'never' covers an idol co-owned with a gentile. Since the Jew worshipped with his own intent, the gentile's ביטול does not help the Jew's share.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי הלל בריה דרבי וולס said: It is needed only where a gentile has a partnership in it. It teaches us that the Jew worships with his own intent.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי הלל answers that 'never' teaches a special case: an idol shared by a Jew and a gentile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think that when the gentile partner nullifies the idol, the whole idol becomes permitted. The word 'never' teaches otherwise, because the Jew's worship comes from his own intent and does not depend on the gentile. So the Jew's share stays forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions use the same case of a shared idol. The first version stresses that the gentile CAN nullify his own share. The second stresses that the Jew's share is NEVER nullified, even by the gentile.
steps.whatToRemember: In a shared idol, the gentile's ביטול works only on his own share. The Jew's share stays forbidden forever, because he worshipped with his own intent.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי הִילֵּל בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי וָולֶס:
phrases.english: Rabbi Hillel, son of Rabbi Volas, said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נִצְרְכָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְגוֹי בָּהּ שׁוּתָּפוּת,
phrases.english: It is needed only where a gentile has a partnership in it,
and it teaches us
that the Jew worships with his own intent.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא נִצְרְכָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְגוֹי בָּהּ שׁוּתָּפוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the word 'never'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Never' covers a shared idol: the gentile's ביטול does not release the Jew's share, because the Jew worshipped with his own intent.

steps.title: משנה: acts that nullify an idol
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks how a gentile nullifies an idol. Cutting off the tip of its ear, nose, or finger works. Crushing it also works, even if nothing is removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does he nullify it? If he cut off the tip of its ear, the tip of its nose, or the tip of its finger, or crushed it, even without removing anything, he has nullified it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and lists acts that nullify an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage that shows the gentile has given up on the idol counts as ביטול. Even a small cut works. The משנה adds that crushing works even when no piece is removed, and the גמרא questions that point in step 8.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: How does he nullify it?
phrases.notes: 'He' is the gentile who owns the idol.

phrases.english: If he cut off the tip of its ear,
the tip of its nose, the tip of its finger,

phrases.aramaic: פְּחָסָהּ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא חִיסְּרָהּ — בִּיטְּלָהּ;
phrases.english: or crushed it, even though he did not remove anything, he has nullified it;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins on how ביטול is done.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cutting off any tip of the idol, or crushing it, nullifies it.

steps.title: משנה: insults do not nullify
steps.stepSummary: Spitting at it, urinating at it, dragging it, or throwing dung at it does not nullify the idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he spat in front of it, urinated in front of it, dragged it, or threw dung at it, it is not nullified.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists acts of disrespect that do NOT count as ביטול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These acts insult the idol but do not damage it. The משנה rules that they do not nullify it.
steps.confusionAlert: רָק here means 'spat'. It is not the Hebrew word 'only'.

phrases.english: If he spat in front of it, urinated in front of it,
dragged it, or threw dung at it,
it is not nullified;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with the acts that do nullify.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Insulting the idol without damaging it does not nullify it.

steps.title: משנה: selling or mortgaging the idol
steps.stepSummary: רבי says selling or mortgaging the idol nullifies it. חכמים say it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold it or mortgaged it, רבי says he nullified it, and the חכמים say he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with a dispute over whether selling or pawning the idol counts as ביטול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the gentile gives the idol up through a business deal, not by damaging it. רבי counts that as ביטול, and חכמים do not.
steps.whatToRemember: Damage nullifies an idol, but insults do not. Selling or mortgaging it is disputed between רבי and חכמים.

phrases.english: If he sold it or mortgaged it,
Rabbi says: he nullified it,
and the Rabbis say: he did not nullify it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a disputed case to the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dispute: רבי says selling or mortgaging nullifies the idol; חכמים say it does not.

steps.title: How does crushing nullify if nothing was removed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how crushing the idol nullifies it when no part was removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: When he did not remove anything, how did he nullify it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה by questioning the crushing case. This sets up רב זירא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other acts in the משנה remove a piece of the idol. Crushing removes nothing, so it is unclear what change counts as ביטול.

phrases.english: GEMARA: When he did not remove anything,
by what did he nullify it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the crushing case from the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of crushing counts as ביטול when nothing is removed?

steps.title: He crushed its face
steps.stepSummary: רב זירא explains that the משנה means he crushed the idol's face.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זירא said: It is where he crushed its face.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זירא answers that the crushing in the משנה is crushing the idol's face.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Crushing the face ruins the idol's form even though nothing is taken away, and that is why it counts as ביטול.

phrases.english: Rav Zeira said:
It is where he crushed its face.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the crushing case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה means crushing the idol's face, which ruins its form.

steps.title: Where do we learn that spitting at an idol does not nullify it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of spitting or urinating before an idol and asks for the source that this does not nullify it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he spat in front of it or urinated in front of it, the idol is not nullified. Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and asks for its source. This sets up חזקיה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spitting and urinating look like clear acts of disrespect, so you might think they show the gentile has given up on the idol. The גמרא wants a source showing that this kind of insult does not count as nullifying it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things learned?

phrases.english: If he spat before it, or urinated before it.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה in step 6. The idol is not nullified in this case.

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's ruling in step 6 and asks for its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that disrespectful acts like spitting do not nullify an idol.

steps.title: חזקיה: an angry person curses his god but then goes back to it
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה brings פסוקים from ישעיהו. A person may curse his god in anger, but afterward he looks back down to the earth, meaning he returns to his idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: The פסוק says, 'When he is hungry, he will get angry and curse his king and his god, and turn upward.' The next פסוק says, 'And he will look to the earth, and see trouble and darkness.' This teaches that even though he cursed his king and his god and turned upward, he will still look back to the earth.
steps.whatsHappening: חזקיה answers the question from step 10. The פסוקים show that insulting an idol in anger does not mean the worshipper has truly given it up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק describes someone cursing his god when things go badly. The next פסוק shows that he goes back to it afterward. So spitting or urinating is only a moment of anger, not a real decision to stop worshipping the idol, and it does not nullify it.

keyTerms.meaning: He will look to the earth, meaning he goes back to his old ways

steps.whatToRemember: Insulting an idol in a moment of anger is temporary, so it does not nullify the idol.

phrases.english: Ḥizkiyya says: As the verse states:
“And it shall come to pass that, when he shall be hungry, he shall fret,
and curse his king and his god,
and turn his face upward.”
And it is written after it:
“And he shall look to the earth,
and behold distress and darkness, etc.”

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּקִלֵּל מַלְכּוֹ וֵאלֹהָיו
phrases.english: That is, even though he cursed his king and his god,
and turned his face upward,
he still looks to the earth.
phrases.notes: He means that afterward the person goes right back to his idol.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question from step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פסוקים in ישעיהו show that an angry worshipper who curses his god later returns to it, so insults do not nullify an idol.

steps.title: Two opinions on when רבי and חכמים argue about selling an idol
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's argument about selling an idol. Two אמוראים disagree: one says the argument is about selling to a non-Jewish smith, and the other says it is about selling to a Jewish smith.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he sold it or mortgaged it, רבי says he nullified it. זעירי quoted רבי יוחנן, and רבי ירמיה בר אבא quoted רב. One said: the argument is when he sold it to a non-Jewish smith, but if he sold it to a Jewish smith, everyone agrees he nullified it. The other said: the argument is when he sold it to a Jewish smith.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about selling an idol and brings two opinions about which case רבי and חכמים are arguing over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Jewish smith will surely melt the idol down, so selling to him clearly shows the gentile is giving it up. The first opinion therefore says everyone agrees in that case, and they only argue about a non-Jewish smith. The second opinion says that even when the buyer is a Jewish smith, the argument still exists.

keyTerms.meaning: He gave it as a pledge for a loan
A smith who melts down metal

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not say which אמורא held which opinion. It only uses 'one said' and 'the other said' (חד אמר).

phrases.english: If he sold it or mortgaged it,
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה in step 7.

phrases.english: Rabbi says: He nullified it, etc.
Ze’eiri says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says that Rav says:
One says: The dispute is when he sold it to a gentile smith,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּצוֹרֵף יִשְׂרָאֵל — דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל בִּיטֵּל,
phrases.english: but when he sold it to a Jewish smith, everyone agrees he nullified it,
And one says: The dispute is when he sold it to a Jewish smith.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְכָרָהּ אוֹ מִשְׁכְּנָהּ, רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: בִּיטֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the spitting case to the משנה's next case, selling the idol, from step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: they argue only about a gentile smith, and everyone agrees that selling to a Jewish smith nullifies the idol. Second opinion: they argue even about a Jewish smith.

steps.title: Does the second opinion also apply the argument to a non-Jewish smith?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to understand the second opinion: is the argument only about a Jewish smith, with everyone agreeing that selling to a non-Jewish smith does not nullify the idol, or do they argue in both cases?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Is the argument only about a Jewish smith, while for a non-Jewish smith everyone agrees he did not nullify it? Or maybe they argue in both cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about the second opinion from step 12. It asks how far the argument between רבי and חכמים reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second opinion only said 'they argue about a Jewish smith.' Maybe this means a non-Jewish smith is an easier case, where everyone agrees the idol is not nullified. Or maybe it means that they argue about a non-Jewish smith as well, so רבי would say that even selling to a non-Jewish smith nullifies the idol.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the חכמים
Both in this case and in that case

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
Is the dispute only about a Jewish smith,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל צוֹרֵף גּוֹי דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל לֹא בִּיטֵּל,
phrases.english: but with a gentile smith everyone agrees he did not nullify it,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא בֵּין בָּזֶה וּבֵין בָּזֶה מַחְלוֹקֶת?
phrases.english: or perhaps there is a dispute both in this case and in that case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to understand the second opinion in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Under the second opinion, is selling to a gentile smith a case where everyone agrees the idol is not nullified, or is it also part of the argument?

steps.title: A ברייתא of רבי is brought to answer the question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי: my view seems right when the idol was sold to destroy it, and my colleagues' view seems right when it was sold to worship it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי said, 'My words seem right when he sold it to destroy it, and my colleagues' words seem right when he sold it to worship it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the question from the last step. This step only quotes the source; the next steps work out what it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי holds that selling the idol is a ביטול, and the חכמים say it is not. Here רבי seems to split the cases: his view fits one kind of sale, and his colleagues' view fits another. The גמרא now has to figure out what 'to destroy it' and 'to worship it' mean.

keyTerms.meaning: My colleagues, meaning the חכמים who argue with רבי

phrases.english: Come and hear, as רבי said:
My words seem right when he sold it to destroy it,
phrases.notes: 'My words' means רבי's view from the משנה that selling the idol cancels its status.

phrases.english: and my colleagues' words when he sold it to worship it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to answer the question raised in step 13
steps.raayaObject: Whether the dispute covers both a Jewish smith and a non-Jewish smith

steps.title: The literal reading of the ברייתא does not work
steps.stepSummary: If 'to destroy' and 'to worship' are meant literally, nobody would argue, so the words must mean something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'to destroy it' mean, and what does 'to worship it' mean? If you say 'to destroy it' means he really bought it to destroy it, and 'to worship it' means he really bought it to worship it, then what is the reason of the one who says it is cancelled, and what is the reason of the one who says it is not cancelled?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא's words mean and shows that the plain reading cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller knew the buyer would really worship it, why would anyone say the idol's status is cancelled? And if the buyer would really destroy it, why would anyone say it is not cancelled? A literal reading leaves no room for a real dispute, so the גמרא needs another meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: He cancelled the idol's forbidden status

phrases.english: What is 'to destroy it' and what is 'to worship it'?
If you say 'to destroy it' means really to destroy it,
and 'to worship it' means really to worship it,
what is the reason of the one who says it is cancelled,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי טַעְמָא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר לֹא בִּיטֵּל?
phrases.english: and what is the reason of the one who says it is not cancelled?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the ברייתא's words mean and rules out the literal reading
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'to destroy it' and 'to worship it' mean in the ברייתא

steps.title: Reading the ברייתא as a Jewish smith versus a non-Jewish smith
steps.stepSummary: 'To destroy' means a Jewish smith, who will probably destroy it, and 'to worship' means a non-Jewish smith, who will probably worship it. So there is a dispute in both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it that 'to destroy it' means to someone who will destroy it later, and who is that? A Jewish smith. 'To worship it' means to someone who will worship it later, and who is that? A non-Jewish smith. Learn from this that there is a dispute both in this case and in that case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a better reading and uses it to finish the proof: they argue about both kinds of smiths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer's plans are not known for sure. We only know what he will probably do. A צורף ישראל will probably destroy the idol, and a צורף גוי will probably worship it. Since רבי gives one case to his own view and the other to his colleagues, it looks as if both sides argue in both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't it that: the גמרא is offering a better reading

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו לְחַבְּלָהּ — לְמִי שֶׁעָתִיד לְחַבְּלָהּ,
phrases.english: Rather, isn't 'to destroy it' to someone who will destroy it later,
and who is that? A Jewish smith.
'To worship it' is to someone who will worship it later,
and who is that? A non-Jewish smith.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: בֵּין בָּזֶה וּבֵין בָּזֶה מַחְלוֹקֶת.
phrases.english: And learn from this: in both this case and that case there is a dispute.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected literal reading and draws the proof from the ברייתא
steps.raayaObject: That the dispute covers both a Jewish smith and a non-Jewish smith
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי's ברייתא, read as a Jewish smith versus a non-Jewish smith

steps.title: The proof is pushed off: the colleagues agree about a Jewish smith
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא really means that even רבי's colleagues accept his view for a Jewish smith. They argue only about a non-Jewish smith.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, this is what it means: רבי said, 'My words seem right to my colleagues when he sold it to destroy it,' meaning to a Jewish smith. Even my colleagues only argued with me when he sold it to worship it, but when it was sold to destroy it, they agree with me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading רבי's words in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reading adds one word: 'my words seem right to my colleagues.' Now the ברייתא does not describe two separate disputes. It says everyone agrees that selling to a צורף ישראל cancels the idol, and the argument is only about a צורף גוי. So the ברייתא no longer proves there is a dispute in both cases.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא can be read as 'even my colleagues agree with me about a צורף ישראל'. Read that way, it matches the first opinion in step 12, so it does not prove that רבי and the חכמים argue in both cases. The question from step 13 is not settled by this ברייתא.
steps.confusionAlert: The new reading changes who 'my words seem right' is aimed at. It is not 'my view versus theirs.' It is 'even they agree with my view' in the case of a Jewish smith.

phrases.english: No, this is what it means:
רבי said: my words seem right to my colleagues
when he sold it to destroy it.
And who is that? A Jewish smith,
because even my colleagues did not argue with me
except when he sold it to worship it,
but when it was to destroy it, they agree with me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 16 by reading the ברייתא differently
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The conclusion that there is a dispute in both cases
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as 'even my colleagues agree with me about a Jewish smith,' so it does not show two separate disputes

steps.title: A ברייתא about scrap metal with an idol inside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: a Jew bought scrap metal from non-Jews and found an idol in it. If he pulled it before paying, he returns it. If he pulled it after paying, he must throw it into the ים המלח.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: Someone buys broken metal pieces from non-Jews and finds an idol among them. If he pulled the goods before he paid, he gives the idol back. If he pulled the goods after he paid, he must take the idol and throw it into the ים המלח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the first opinion in step 12, that everyone agrees selling to a צורף ישראל cancels the idol. This step only quotes the source. The next step explains why it is a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key point is that even after a Jew bought the idol from the non-Jew, the ברייתא still treats it as a forbidden idol that must be destroyed. So the sale to a Jew did not cancel it. That sits badly with the idea that a sale to a Jewish smith cancels an idol according to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: He pulled. Pulling an item toward oneself is a way of acquiring it.
The Dead Sea, where forbidden items are thrown so that nobody can benefit from them

phrases.english: They challenged: One who buys broken metal pieces from the non-Jews
and found an idol among them,

phrases.aramaic: אִם עַד שֶׁלֹּא נָתַן מָעוֹת מָשַׁךְ — יַחֲזִיר,
phrases.english: if he pulled it before he gave the money, he returns it,
phrases.notes: Pulling is how he takes possession. Here he did it before paying, so the deal can still be undone.

phrases.aramaic: אִם מִשֶּׁנָּתַן מָעוֹת מָשַׁךְ — יוֹלִיךְ לְיָם הַמֶּלַח.
phrases.english: if he pulled it after he gave the money, he must take it to the Dead Sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from רבי's ברייתא fails, the גמרא brings a source that seems to contradict the first opinion in step 12, that everyone agrees a sale to a Jewish smith cancels the idol.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first opinion in step 12: the dispute is only about a gentile smith, and with a Jewish smith everyone agrees the idol is cancelled
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows that an idol sold to a Jew stays forbidden, so the sale did not cancel it.

steps.title: Whose view could the ברייתא follow?
steps.stepSummary: If רבי and the רבנן argue about a Jewish smith, the ברייתא simply follows the רבנן. But if everyone agrees a sale to a Jewish smith cancels the idol, then the ברייתא matches no one.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works fine if you say the argument is about a Jewish smith. Then whose view is this ברייתא? It is the רבנן's. But if you say the argument is only about a non-Jewish smith, and for a Jewish smith everyone agrees he cancelled it, then whose view is this ברייתא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the challenge. Under the first opinion in step 12, nobody would hold that the idol in the ברייתא is still forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second opinion in step 12 places the argument in the case of a Jewish smith, so the ברייתא can follow the רבנן, who say the sale does not cancel the idol. The first opinion says everyone agrees a sale to a Jewish smith cancels it. That leaves no one who matches a ברייתא that forbids the idol after it was sold to a Jew.

keyTerms.meaning: It works fine if you say. This sets up a contrast with a reading that does not work.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא בְּצוֹרֵף יִשְׂרָאֵל מַחְלוֹקֶת,
phrases.english: It works fine if you say there is a dispute about a Jewish smith,
Whose view is this? It is the Rabbis'.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ בְּצוֹרֵף גּוֹי מַחְלוֹקֶת,
phrases.english: But if you say the dispute is about a non-Jewish smith,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּצוֹרֵף יִשְׂרָאֵל דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל בִּיטֵּל,
phrases.english: but with a Jewish smith everyone agrees he cancelled it,
whose view is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא בְּצוֹרֵף יִשְׂרָאֵל מַחְלוֹקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains exactly how the ברייתא from step 18 fits the second opinion in step 12 but creates a problem for the first.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first opinion in step 12: the dispute is only about a gentile smith, and with a Jewish smith everyone agrees the idol is cancelled
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the first opinion in step 12, the ברייתא, which forbids an idol sold to a Jew, follows no known opinion.

steps.title: He only meant to sell scrap metal
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is a different case. The non-Jew sold scrap metal and never knowingly sold an idol, so he never meant to cancel it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because he sold it thinking it was scrap metal. He did not sell it thinking it was an idol.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the ברייתא's case is not a real sale of an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Canceling an idol depends on the non-Jew knowingly giving it up. In the ברייתא he did not know an idol was among the scrap, so selling it shows nothing about his attitude toward the idol. So the first opinion in step 12 still stands: when a non-Jew knowingly sells an idol to a Jewish smith, everyone agrees it is cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: With the understanding of, thinking that

steps.whatToRemember: An idol is cancelled only when the non-Jew knowingly gives it up as an idol. Selling it by accident, hidden in scrap metal, does not count. So the first opinion in step 12 survives the challenge.

phrases.english: It is different there,
since he sold it with the understanding that it was scrap metal,
he did not sell it with the understanding that it was an idol.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 18-19 by separating the ברייתא's case from a knowing sale.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the ברייתא involves a sale made without knowing about the idol
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any sale of an idol to a Jew should count as canceling it, so the ברייתא seemed to contradict the first opinion in step 12.
steps.terutzMaskana: Canceling requires a knowing sale of the idol. The ברייתא's sale was only of scrap, so it does not contradict the first opinion in step 12.

steps.title: New ברייתא: idols that were pawned, buried, stolen, or abandoned
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא lists four cases: a non-Jew borrowed money using the idol as collateral, a rockslide fell on it, robbers stole it, or the owners left it and went overseas. The ruling comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he borrowed money against it, or a rockslide fell on it, or robbers stole it, or the owners left it and went overseas,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new ברייתא and lists the cases first. This step is setting up the ruling, which comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case asks whether the owner has given up on the idol in a way that cancels it. In each one the idol leaves the owner's control or care without a clear statement from him. The ברייתא's answer for these cases has not been given yet.

keyTerms.meaning: He borrowed against it, using it as collateral
A rockslide or collapse of rubble

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If he borrowed against it,
or a rockslide fell on it,
or robbers stole it,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהִנִּיחוּהָ הַבְּעָלִים וְהָלְכוּ לִמְדִינַת הַיָּם,
phrases.english: or the owners left it and went overseas,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: whether an idol is cancelled when it leaves its owner's hands in different ways.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lists four cases (collateral, rockslide, theft, abandonment). The ruling follows in the next part of the text.
